text.content:
# Arogyam Platform — monitoring guide

This dashboard covers both live environments — **aa-stg** (staging) and **aa-prod** (production) — side by side on every tile, so you can always compare current behavior against the same tenant/service in the other environment. The platform is multi-tenant: each hospital/site (tenant) is served by shared infrastructure — one ingress-nginx layer, one HAPI FHIR server, one Keycloak instance, and one Cloud SQL database per environment — partitioned internally by tenant, not by separate infrastructure per tenant.

Sections below run roughly in request order: **Traffic** (the edge, what's coming in) → **Per-tenant** (who it's from) → **Workloads** (is Kubernetes keeping pods healthy) → **HAPI FHIR** and **Keycloak** (the two application services actually serving those requests) → **Nodes** (is there compute headroom) → **Data** (Cloud SQL + GCS) → **Alerts** and **Availability** (what's already firing, and whether the platform is reachable from outside at all).

**New to this system?** A good first move when something looks wrong is to work top to bottom: check Traffic for an obvious spike or 5xx surge, then Workloads for restarts/scheduling problems, then the specific service (HAPI FHIR or Keycloak) for JVM/error signals, then Nodes for a capacity ceiling.

## Traffic — ingress-nginx

Every tile on this dashboard plots **aa-stg and aa-prod side by side** as separate legend series (e.g. "... (aa-stg)" / "... (aa-prod)") rather than a dashboard-wide environment picker — a single Cloud Monitoring template variable could not substitute reliably across every tile shape, so each environment is queried explicitly instead. Source: `prometheus.googleapis.com/nginx_ingress_controller_*`, scraped live from ingress-nginx via GMP in both environments. This is the first place to look for a platform-wide incident: a request-rate cliff means nothing is getting through; a 5xx spike above the 2%/10% thresholds means the platform is up but failing requests.

## Per-tenant traffic — one hostname per tenant

Each tenant (hospital/site) is reached through its own hostname on the shared ingress, so these two tiles break the cluster-wide Traffic numbers above down per tenant. Use this to tell whether a spike or error surge is platform-wide or isolated to one tenant — a single elevated line usually points at that tenant's own usage pattern or a tenant-specific data issue, not an infra-wide problem.

text.content:
## Workloads — GKE system metrics

Sourced from GKE's built-in `kubernetes.io/*` metrics (not the Prometheus/GMP scrape used in the sections below). This is the Kubernetes-level view of whether pods are actually staying up and scheduled: restarts, CPU/memory pressure against configured limits, and available replicas per deployment. A deployment repeatedly restarting or sitting below its expected replica count here — especially alongside a CPU/memory line pinned near 1.0 — usually means a pod can't get scheduled or is being OOM-killed, not an application bug. Staging and the ArgoCD hub currently run with no autoscaling headroom, so check the Nodes section below before assuming it's a code problem.

## HAPI FHIR — /actuator/prometheus

HAPI FHIR is the clinical data server — every FHIR resource read/write for every tenant goes through it, so this section is the closest thing to an application-health view for the platform's core data path. Standard Micrometer JVM/HTTP metrics, scraped from HAPI's actuator endpoint. The `uri` label is almost always `UNKNOWN` on this deployment, so nothing here groups by endpoint path — only by outcome and method. **Watch for:** heap that climbs and never drops back after GC (possible leak or undersized heap), a rising GC pause rate (JVM under memory pressure), or a growing share of non-2xx outcomes in the request-rate tile.

## Keycloak — /auth/realms/master/metrics

Keycloak is the identity provider behind every login on the platform — if it's unhealthy, users can't authenticate even if HAPI FHIR and everything else is fine. Scraped via the aerogear `keycloak-metrics-spi`, which uses classic prometheus-client metric naming — different from the Micrometer names in the HAPI FHIR section above, so the two JVM heap tiles measure the same underlying thing but under different metric names. **Watch for:** the error ratio crossing its 2%/10% thresholds, or a rising p95/p99 that would show up to users as slow logins.

text.content:
## Nodes — allocatable vs. committed

The raw compute-capacity view: how much of each node's allocatable CPU/memory is already committed by pod requests, independent of whether those pods are actually using it. Staging and the ArgoCD hub currently run a single node each with `node_max_count=1` in Terraform — no further autoscaling headroom — so these tiles are the early warning for the exact failure mode that has already happened once on this platform: a new deployment unable to schedule because existing pods have already claimed the node's capacity. **If either line crosses the 0.9 threshold**, a new pod won't schedule until something is deleted/scaled down, or `node_max_count` is raised (`terraform/modules/gke-cluster`).

## Data — Cloud SQL + per-tenant GCS

Cloud SQL holds every tenant's clinical (HAPI FHIR) and identity (Keycloak) data in one shared Postgres instance per environment; GCS holds per-tenant media/attachments in one bucket per tenant. Filtered on `database_id` / bucket name rather than a cluster label, since neither resource type carries one. **Watch for:** CPU/disk utilisation approaching its 0.85 threshold (production is REGIONAL/HA with daily PITR backups; staging is ZONAL with shorter retention — see `docs/monitoring.md`), and connection count trending toward Cloud SQL's connection limit. Replication lag is expected to always read no data — see that tile's own note.

widget.title: Cloud SQL CPU + disk utilisation (aa-stg + aa-prod)
Cloud SQL replication lag (aa-stg + aa-prod) — expected to show no data; neither environment runs a read replica (docs/monitoring.md)
GCS per-tenant bucket object count (aa-stg + aa-prod)
GCS per-tenant bucket total size (aa-stg + aa-prod)

text.content:
## Alerts

What's currently configured to page or notify, and where to go to see what's actually firing right now.

This platform's alert policies — error ratios, latency, node capacity, TLS cert expiry, and more — are all defined in `terraform/envs/monitoring/alerts.tf`, not as individual tiles here. Cloud Monitoring's dashboard widgets can only bind to one named policy at a time, and policy IDs aren't known until after `terraform apply`, so a live embedded incident list isn't practical from this file.

**To triage an alert:** open [Alerting incidents](https://console.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerting/incidents?project=your-gcp-project-id), filtered by the `env` label (`aa-stg` / `aa-prod`), or browse [all policies](https://console.cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerting/policies?project=your-gcp-project-id) directly.

Want a per-policy incident tile instead? Add one `alertChart` tile per policy once `terraform apply` has produced real policy IDs (`terraform output`, or `google_monitoring_alert_policy.<name>["aa-stg"].name`).

## Availability — synthetic uptime + internal health probes

Two different checks live in this section: **external synthetic uptime checks** against the platform's public hostnames (top row) and arogyam-dashboard's own **internal health probe** (bottom row, blackbox-exporter based, scraped like any other in-cluster target). This is the only external, black-box view on the dashboard — it reflects what a real user or API client would see, independent of whether anything inside the cluster reports itself healthy.

**Public hostname checks** back the `cert_expiry` alert policy (`terraform/envs/monitoring/alerts.tf`) and are filtered on the literal configured hostname rather than the uptime check's generated ID, which is only known after `terraform apply`. **Status: currently show no data** — they depend on a DNS fix that is still an open ask with the platform team (`docs/deployment-guide.md (prerequisites)` §5). Until that's resolved, this platform has no working external uptime signal.

**Internal probe** is confirmed live and working — a real value here is your fastest signal that arogyam-dashboard itself is reachable and responding from inside the cluster.
